title: Irrationality of √p for Any Prime p (From Axioms)
description: Generalizes the √2 irrationality proof to all primes: for any prime p, there are no coprime a, b with a² = p·b². Built from scratch using Euclid's criterion for primality.

overview.historicalContext:
The irrationality of $\sqrt{2}$ was first proved by the ancient Greeks, traditionally attributed to Hippasus of Metapontum (~500 BCE). According to legend, Hippasus was drowned at sea by fellow Pythagoreans for revealing that $\sqrt{2}$ is incommensurable with 1, shattering their belief that all quantities are ratios of whole numbers.

The proof by contradiction—assuming $\sqrt{2} = a/b$ in lowest terms and deriving that both $a$ and $b$ must be even—is one of the most celebrated arguments in mathematics. Theodorus of Cyrene (~465–398 BCE) extended the result to $\sqrt{3}, \sqrt{5}, \ldots, \sqrt{17}$ (as reported in Plato's *Theaetetus*), though his methods are debated. His student Theaetetus provided a general classification: $\sqrt{n}$ is irrational whenever $n$ is not a perfect square.

The key insight enabling the generalization is Euclid's lemma (Elements VII.30, ~300 BCE): if a prime divides a product, it divides one of the factors. This property was used implicitly in the $\sqrt{2}$ proof (the "even/odd" trick) but Euclid recognized it as a general property of primes. In modern algebra, this multiplicative property is taken as the *definition* of a prime element in a ring, distinguishing it from the weaker notion of irreducibility.

This formalization makes the connection explicit by defining primality via Euclid's criterion rather than the divisor property, revealing why the $\sqrt{2}$ proof generalizes immediately to all primes.
overview.problemStatement:
**Open Question**: Can the pedagogical $\sqrt{2}$ irrationality proof be generalized to $\sqrt{p}$ for any prime $p$?

**Answer**: Yes. The proof structure is identical once we replace 'even/odd' (divisibility by 2) with 'divisible by $p$ / not divisible by $p$'. The key ingredient is Euclid's lemma: $p \mid n^2 \Rightarrow p \mid n$ for prime $p$.

We formalize this completely from scratch, building divisibility, primality, and the main theorem without relying on Mathlib's number theory.
overview.text: Generalizes the √2 irrationality proof to all primes: for any prime p, there are no coprime a, b with a² = p·b². Built from scratch using Euclid's criterion for primality.
overview.proofStrategy:
The proof generalizes the classical $\sqrt{2}$ argument in three steps:

1. **Define EuclidPrime**: $p > 1$ and $p \mid ab \Rightarrow p \mid a \lor p \mid b$
2. **Key lemma**: $p$ prime, $p \mid n^2 \Rightarrow p \mid n$ (trivial from definition since $n^2 = n \cdot n$)
3. **Main theorem**: If $a^2 = p \cdot b^2$ with $b > 0$, then $p \mid a$ and $p \mid b$ (so $a/b$ is not in lowest terms)

The magic is step 2: with Euclid's criterion as the *definition* of prime, the key lemma that took 20 lines for $p=2$ becomes a one-liner for all primes.
keyInsights: **The even/odd trick IS Euclid's lemma for p=2**: The parent proof's 'n² even implies n even' is exactly the statement '2 | n² implies 2 | n', which is Euclid's lemma for the prime 2

**The right definition of prime**: For irrationality proofs, the multiplicative property (Euclid's criterion) is more natural than the divisor property. The two are equivalent via Bezout's identity, but the multiplicative form directly gives the key lemma

**From 20 lines to 2 lines**: The parent proof needs Even/Odd definitions, parity lemmas, and case analysis to prove 'n² even implies n even'. With Euclid's criterion, this becomes: p | n*n implies p | n or p | n, so p | n. QED.
**Modular arithmetic verification**: Small primes (2, 3, 5) are verified as EuclidPrime by checking that nonzero residues mod p form a multiplicative group (no zero divisors)

**Prime vs irreducible distinction**: In general rings, "prime" (Euclid's criterion: p | ab → p | a or p | b) and "irreducible" (only trivial factorizations) are different properties. They coincide for ℕ (and all UFDs), but this proof reveals that it is the *prime* property—not irreducibility—that drives irrationality arguments

sections.title: Divisibility (Built from Scratch)
sections.summary: Defines `Divides p n` as $\exists k, n = p \cdot k$ with basic lemmas: every number divides 0 and itself, divisibility through multiplication, and small numbers less than $p$ are not divisible by $p$

sections.title: Primality via Euclid's Criterion
sections.summary: Defines `EuclidPrime p` as $p > 1$ and $p \mid ab \Rightarrow p \mid a \lor p \mid b$. This is the exact property needed for irrationality proofs, equivalent to classical primality via Bezout's identity

sections.title: Verifying Small Primes
sections.summary: Proves 2, 3, and 5 satisfy Euclid's criterion using modular arithmetic (`Nat.mul_mod`). For prime $p$, the verification reduces to checking that $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ has no zero divisors

sections.title: Bridge to Mathlib
sections.summary: Proves every `Nat.Prime` is an `EuclidPrime`, connecting our from-axioms development to Mathlib's library for users who need the classical definition

sections.title: Key Lemma: Prime Divides Square Implies Divides Base
sections.summary: Proves $p$ prime and $p \mid n^2 \Rightarrow p \mid n$. With Euclid's criterion as definition, this is a two-line proof: $p \mid n \cdot n$ gives $p \mid n \lor p \mid n$, so $p \mid n$

sections.title: Coprimality Modulo p
sections.summary: Defines \ as ¬(p | a ∧ p | b)—a weaker form of coprimality that generalizes "not both even" from the √2 proof. Full coprimality (gcd = 1) would require building GCD from scratch

sections.title: Main Theorem: √p is Irrational
sections.summary: Proves that for any Euclid prime $p$, if $a^2 = p \cdot b^2$ with $b > 0$, then $p$ divides both $a$ and $b$. Includes helper lemmas for the arithmetic cancellation step ($p^2k^2 = pb^2 \Rightarrow pk^2 = b^2$)

sections.title: Concrete Instances and Applications
sections.summary: Derives $\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{3}$, $\sqrt{5}$ irrationality as immediate corollaries, plus a general bridge theorem for any Mathlib-certified prime

sections.title: Alternative Contrapositive Formulation
sections.summary: Restates the main theorem without coprimality: if $a^2 = pb^2$, then either $b = 0$ or $p$ divides both $a$ and $b$. This contrapositive form eliminates the need for a CoprimeMod hypothesis

sections.title: Educational Notes and Extensions
sections.summary: Documents the correspondence between the √2 and √p proofs, explains the relationship between Euclid's criterion and the classical prime definition via Bézout's identity, and discusses limitations for non-prime radicands like √6

conclusion.summary: The irrationality of √p for prime p is proved completely from scratch, revealing that the classical √2 proof secretly uses Euclid's lemma. By defining primality via the multiplicative property (Euclid's criterion), the key lemma becomes trivial and the proof generalizes to all primes with zero additional effort.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: **Key correspondence:**

| √2 proof concept | General √p concept |
|---|---|
| n is even | p divides n |
| n is odd | p does not divide n |
| n² even → n even | p | n² → p | n (Euclid) |
| coprime = not both even | coprime = not both div by p |

The generalization shows that parity is not the essential ingredient—primality is.

**Broader Connections**: This is the same insight that drives modern algebraic number theory: the prime elements of a ring (those satisfying Euclid's criterion) are the building blocks of its multiplicative structure. In a unique factorization domain, prime and irreducible elements coincide, but the *prime* property is what makes descent arguments work.
openQuestions: Prove equivalence of Euclid's criterion with the classical prime definition (requires building Bézout's identity from scratch—see the gallery's bezout-identity formalization)
Extend to √n for any non-square n (requires unique factorization: if n = p₁^{a₁} · ··· · pₖ^{aₖ} with some aᵢ odd, then √n is irrational)
Build the p-adic valuation vₚ from scratch and prove vₚ(ab) = vₚ(a) + vₚ(b), giving a one-line irrationality proof: vₚ(√p) = 1/2 ∉ ℤ
Formalize the converse: every EuclidPrime satisfies the classical prime definition (requires Bézout's identity in the opposite direction)

crossReferences.description: This proof generalizes the parent √2 formalization to all primes, replacing Even/Odd with general divisibility by p
Uses Mathlib's irrational_sqrt_natCast_iff for a different approach to square root irrationality, covering non-square composites as well
Bézout's identity is the key theorem needed to prove equivalence of Euclid's criterion with the classical prime definition, which this proof deliberately avoids
The nth root irrationality proof extends beyond square roots, using similar descent arguments for higher powers
Both proofs rely on fundamental properties of prime numbers—this one uses the multiplicative (Euclid) property, while infinitude uses the divisor property
